runtime_row.subject: Science
runtime_row.subtopic: Human Eye Structure, Defects of Vision
runtime_row.questionText:
Case Study: Rajesh, a 45-year-old man, visits an eye clinic complaining that he can see distant objects clearly but has difficulty reading newspapers. His daughter, who is 12 years old, complains that she cannot see the board at school clearly but can read books comfortably. Both require different types of lenses for correction.

Question 1: What is the vision defect of Rajesh? What type of lens would he need?
Question 2: Identify the vision defect of Rajesh's daughter and suggest an appropriate lens type.
Question 3: Explain the role of the ciliary muscles in accommodation and why it fails in Rajesh's case.
runtime_row.answer: 1) Rajesh has presbyopia; needs convex lens. 2) Daughter has myopia; needs concave lens. 3) Ciliary muscles adjust lens shape for accommodation. In presbyopia, aging reduces lens elasticity and ciliary muscle efficiency.
solutionSteps: Question 1 Analysis:
- Rajesh can see distant objects clearly (normal for distance)
- Difficulty reading newspapers indicates near vision problem
- At age 45, this is presbyopia due to lens elasticity loss
- Convex lens is needed to converge light for near objects
Question 2 Analysis:
- Daughter cannot see distant board clearly (myopia)
- Can read books (normal for near)
- Concave lens is required to diverge light rays
- This brings the focal point forward onto the retina
Question 3 Analysis:
- Ciliary muscles control lens shape through contraction and relaxation
- For near vision, ciliary muscles contract, making lens more convex
- In presbyopia, the lens loses elasticity and cannot change shape effectively
- Aging reduces ciliary muscle efficiency and lens accommodation capacity
runtime_row.finalAnswer: 1) Rajesh has presbyopia; needs convex lens. 2) Daughter has myopia; needs concave lens. 3) Ciliary muscles adjust lens shape for accommodation. In presbyopia, aging reduces lens elasticity and ciliary muscle efficiency.

runtime_row.subject: Science
runtime_row.subtopic: Dispersion of white light through a prism
runtime_row.questionText: When white light is incident on one of the refracting surfaces of a prism, the light diverges into its constituent colours violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange and red. This splitting of white light into its seven constituent colours is called dispersion, and the band of colours obtained on a screen is the spectrum. Red colour bends the least and violet bends the most on passing through the prism. Answer: a. What will happen when a red-coloured light is passed through a prism? b. Which type of spectrum is produced by white light when it is passed through a glass prism? c. Why does red light bend the least while violet light bends the most during dispersion? [OR] c. Explain the cause of dispersion of white light through a prism.
runtime_row.answer: a. Red light does not split into any constituent colours on passing through the prism. b. White light through a glass prism gives an impure spectrum (overlapping colours). c. Violet has the slowest speed in glass and red the fastest; lower speed means greater bending, so violet bends most and red least. [OR c. Dispersion occurs because different colours travel at different speeds in the same medium, so they have different refrangibility and separate out.]
solutionSteps: [1 mark] a. A red-coloured (monochromatic) light will not split into any constituent colours on passing through the prism (it only deviates as a single colour).
[1 mark] b. White light passed through a glass prism produces an impure spectrum, in which the different colours overlap.
[1 mark] c. In VIBGYOR, violet has the slowest speed and red the fastest speed in glass; the slower a colour travels, the more it bends.

[1 mark] c. Therefore red (fastest) bends the least and violet (slowest) bends the most during dispersion. [OR c. Dispersion is caused because the different component colours of light travel at different speeds in the same medium (different refrangibility), so they deviate by different amounts and separate.]
runtime_row.finalAnswer: a. Red light does not split. b. Impure spectrum. c. Violet (slowest) bends most, red (fastest) bends least (OR dispersion is due to different speeds/refrangibility of colours in the medium).

runtime_row.question:
Anita's grandmother cannot see nearby objects clearly. Her doctor prescribed spectacles with convex lenses of power +2.5 D.
(a) Name the eye defect the grandmother is suffering from.
(b) What causes this defect?
(c) Calculate the focal length of the prescribed lens.
(d) Draw a ray diagram to show how this lens corrects the defect.

(c) f = 1/P = 1/2.5 = 0.4 m = 40 cm. (d) Convex lens converges light rays before they enter the eye, shifting the image to the retina.

runtime_row.questionText: Refer to the heart diagram (chambers numbered 6, 7, 8, 9; structure 12 labelled). (a) Which chamber pumps blood to the lungs for oxygenation? Name the blood vessels that carry this blood to the lungs. (b) Identify the structure at number 12 and state its function. (c) Why do chambers 6 and 7 have thicker muscular walls than chambers 8 and 9? Name each of these chambers.
runtime_row.answer: (a) Chamber 7 = right ventricle; vessels = pulmonary arteries. (b) Valves — prevent backflow. (c) Ventricles pump blood out at high pressure.
solutionSteps: [1 mark] (a) Chamber 7 = RIGHT VENTRICLE pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs through the PULMONARY ARTERIES.
[1 mark] (b) Structure 12 = valve(s); function: ensure that blood does not flow backwards when the atria or ventricles contract.
[1 mark] (c) Chambers 6 and 7 = LEFT and RIGHT VENTRICLES; chambers 8 and 9 = LEFT and RIGHT ATRIA.
[1 mark] (c) Ventricles have thicker muscular walls because they pump blood out of the heart at high pressure to reach all parts of the body, whereas the atria only push blood into the ventricles.
runtime_row.finalAnswer: (a) Right ventricle → pulmonary arteries; (b) valves prevent backflow; (c) ventricles (6,7) thicker than atria (8,9) — pump at high pressure.

runtime_row.subject: Science
runtime_row.questionText: Explain the process of nutrition in Amoeba.
runtime_row.answer: Amoeba is a unicellular heterotroph. Steps: (1) INGESTION: Amoeba sees food (smaller organisms/particles), extends pseudopodia (false feet) around it, surrounding and engulfing it to form a FOOD VACUOLE. (2) DIGESTION: Digestive enzymes (from cytoplasm) are secreted into the vacuole; food is broken down chemically into simple, absorbable molecules. (3) ABSORPTION: Simple molecules pass through vacuole membrane into the cytoplasm. (4) ASSIMILATION: Cells use these absorbed nutrients for energy, growth, repair. (5) EGESTION: Undigested waste is removed from the cell by rupture of the vacuole at the cell surface.
solutionSteps: [1 mark] (1) Ingestion: pseudopodia engulf food forming a food vacuole.
[1 mark] (2) Digestion: enzymes in vacuole break food into simple molecules.
[0.5 mark] (3) Absorption: nutrients move into cytoplasm from vacuole.
[0.5 mark] (4) Assimilation: cell uses nutrients for energy/growth.
[1 mark] (5) Egestion: undigested waste pushed out by vacuole bursting at cell surface.
[1 mark] All five steps occur within a single cell — typical of unicellular heterotrophic nutrition.
runtime_row.finalAnswer: Ingestion (pseudopodia) → digestion (enzymes in vacuole) → absorption → assimilation → egestion (vacuole bursts).

runtime_row.questionText: Discuss how the processes of photosynthesis and respiration sustain life.
runtime_row.answer: Photosynthesis makes food and releases oxygen, letting energy enter food chains; respiration releases that energy for life processes and consumes the oxygen produced.
solutionSteps: [1 mark] Photosynthesis: plants make food / starch, so (light) energy enters food chains.
[1 mark] Consumers eat plants and gain energy from them; oxygen is released in photosynthesis.
[1 mark] Respiration releases energy from food for growth / movement / maintaining body temperature (AVP).
[1 mark] Respiration consumes the oxygen produced by photosynthesis, linking the two processes (ALLOW at least one point from each list).
runtime_row.finalAnswer: Photosynthesis stores energy as food and releases oxygen; respiration releases that energy for life and uses the oxygen — together they sustain life.

runtime_row.subject: Science
runtime_row.questionText: Describe the passage of air through the human respiratory system from the nostrils to the site of gas exchange, and explain how the alveoli are adapted for the efficient exchange of gases.
runtime_row.answer: Air passes nostrils to pharynx to larynx to trachea to bronchi to bronchioles to alveoli; the alveoli are numerous, thin-walled, moist and richly supplied with capillaries, allowing efficient diffusion of gases.
solutionSteps: [1 mark] Air is drawn in through the nostrils into the nasal passage, where it is warmed, moistened and filtered by fine hairs and mucus, and then passes through the pharynx and larynx.

[1 mark] From the larynx the air passes into the trachea (windpipe), which is supported by rings of cartilage that prevent it from collapsing; the trachea divides into two bronchi, one entering each lung.
[1 mark] Within the lungs each bronchus divides repeatedly into finer and finer bronchioles, which finally end in balloon-like air sacs called alveoli, where the exchange of gases takes place.

[1 mark] Adaptations of the alveoli: they are extremely numerous, providing a very large total surface area for gas exchange, and their walls are extremely thin (one cell thick) and are surrounded by a dense network of blood capillaries.

[1 mark] The alveolar surface is moist, so oxygen dissolves and diffuses into the blood (onto haemoglobin) while carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into the alveolar air to be breathed out — the exchange occurring by simple diffusion down the concentration gradients.
runtime_row.finalAnswer: Air travels nostrils to trachea to bronchi to bronchioles to alveoli; the alveoli's large number, thin moist walls and rich capillary supply make gas exchange by diffusion highly efficient.

runtime_row.subject: Science
runtime_row.questionText: Draw a labelled diagram of the human heart and describe its structure. Name its four chambers and the major blood vessels connected to them, explain the function of the valves, and state why the wall of the left ventricle is thicker than that of the right ventricle.
runtime_row.answer: The heart has four chambers (two atria, two ventricles) separated by a septum; the right side handles deoxygenated blood (vena cava, pulmonary artery) and the left handles oxygenated blood (pulmonary vein, aorta); valves ensure one-way flow, and the left ventricle is thicker because it pumps blood to the whole body.
solutionSteps: [1 mark] The human heart is a muscular organ divided into four chambers — two upper thin-walled atria (right and left) and two lower thick-walled ventricles (right and left); a muscular septum separates the right side from the left side so that oxygenated and deoxygenated blood do not mix.
[1 mark] The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the body through the vena cava, and the right ventricle pumps this blood through the pulmonary artery to the lungs.
[1 mark] The left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the lungs through the pulmonary vein, and the left ventricle pumps this blood through the aorta to the whole body.

[1 mark] Valves — present between each atrium and its ventricle and at the bases of the aorta and pulmonary artery — allow blood to flow in only one direction and prevent it flowing backward when the chambers contract.

[1 mark] The left ventricle has a thicker muscular wall than the right ventricle because it has to pump blood at high pressure to the entire body (systemic circulation), whereas the right ventricle only pumps blood a short distance to the nearby lungs.
runtime_row.finalAnswer: Four chambers separated by a septum, with vena cava/pulmonary artery on the right and pulmonary vein/aorta on the left; valves give one-way flow, and the left ventricle is thickest as it pumps to the whole body.
runtime_row.diagramDescription: Human heart in frontal (vertical) section showing the four chambers labelled right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium and left ventricle, separated by the septum; superior and inferior vena cava entering the right atrium, the pulmonary artery leaving the right ventricle towards the lungs, pulmonary veins entering the left atrium, and the aorta arching out of the left ventricle; atrioventricular (bicuspid and tricuspid) valves between atria and ventricles and the semilunar valves at the artery bases; the wall of the left ventricle drawn distinctly thicker than that of the right ventricle.

runtime_row.questionText: a. How is oxygen and carbon dioxide exchanged between blood and tissue? How are the gases transported in human being? b. What is haemoglobin? [CBSE 2016-17]
runtime_row.answer: a. Exchange of gases in tissues occurs through diffusion. Oxygen is carried as oxyhaemoglobin from lungs to tissues. It dissociates and carbon dioxide diffuses out into blood from tissues. It is transported in dissolved form and reaches lungs where again it diffuses to alveoli. b
solutionSteps: [3 marks] a. Exchange of gases in tissues occurs through diffusion. Oxygen is carried as oxyhaemoglobin from lungs to tissues. It dissociates and carbon dioxide diffuses out into blood from tissues. It is transported in dissolved form and reaches lungs where again it diffuses to alveoli. b. Respiratory pigment: Haemoglobin is a red coloured protein present in red blood cells. Haemoglobin has affinity for O2.

runtime_row.subject: Science
runtime_row.questionText: There are two conducting tissues of plants: first is xylem and second is phloem. Tracheids and vessels which are two kinds of elements of xylem. 3. Tracheids are found in all vascular plants. They are spindle shaped, have only pits and are not very efficient. 4. Vessels are found in flowering plants, are tube like, have perforation plates and pits making them more efficient. 5. When loss of water in vapour occur from leaves of plants due to transpiration, deficit of water is created in the leaves. Evaporation of water molecules from the cells of a leaf creates a suction force which pulls water from the xylem cells. 6. Water and minerals dissolved in it move up to leaves from root through tracheids and vessels, pulling water and minerals upward through xylem elements-ascent of sap. Thus transpiration helps in upward movement of water from roots to leaves. 7. The roots of a plant absorb water and dissolved substances from the soil, which is needed by the aerial parts of the plants. As such these substances are to be transported from roots up to stem, leaves and flowers. 80. Describe the mechanism of gaseous exchange in tissues and lungs. [Delhi 2015] or How is oxygen and carbon dioxide transported in human being? [CBSE 2016] or How is oxygen and carbon dioxide transported in human being? Explain clearly how the air is inhaled and exhaled during breathing in humans.
runtime_row.answer: [All India 2009] Exchange of gases in tissues: a. Most of oxygen is carried by haemoglobin in blood. On reaching the tissues, it gets diffused into the cells as it is in higher concentration than in the cells. b. The carbon dioxide, which is formed in the cells, gets accumulated
solutionSteps: [1 mark] Transport of oxygen: Oxygen from the alveoli of the lungs diffuses into the blood and is carried mainly by haemoglobin in the red blood cells as oxyhaemoglobin; in the tissues, where oxygen concentration is lower, it dissociates and diffuses into the cells.

[1 mark] Transport of carbon dioxide: Carbon dioxide produced in the tissues is at a higher concentration than in the blood, so it diffuses into the blood and is transported mostly dissolved in the blood plasma to the lungs, from where it is expelled during exhalation.

[1 mark] Inhalation (breathing in): The diaphragm and the rib (intercostal) muscles contract — the diaphragm flattens and the ribs move up and outward — enlarging the thoracic cavity; the pressure inside falls and air rushes into the lungs.
[1 mark] Exhalation (breathing out): The diaphragm and rib muscles relax, the thoracic cavity decreases in volume, the pressure rises above atmospheric pressure and air is pushed out of the lungs.

[1 mark] Exchange surface: In the alveoli, the large surface area and rich blood supply allow efficient diffusion of oxygen into the blood and carbon dioxide out of it, completing the exchange of gases.

runtime_row.subject: Science
runtime_row.question:
A student performed an experiment to show that CO₂ is necessary for photosynthesis. A potted plant was kept in the dark for 48 hours, then a leaf was enclosed in a flask containing KOH.
(a) Why was the plant kept in the dark for 48 hours?
(b) What is the role of KOH in the experiment?
(c) After exposing the plant to sunlight, what result would be observed on testing the enclosed leaf with iodine?
(d) Write the balanced chemical equation for photosynthesis.
runtime_row.answer: (a) To destarch the leaves — ensure no pre-existing starch. (b) KOH absorbs CO₂, making the flask CO₂-free. (c) The leaf would not turn blue-black, indicating no starch was produced. (d) 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ (in presence of sunlight and chlorophyll).
runtime_row.explanation: Classic photosynthesis experiment — frequently asked as case-based.

runtime_row.questionText: A student has obtained a magnified image of a flame on a screen using a convex lens. To draw the corresponding ray diagram, to show the image formation, which of the following two rays whose paths after refraction are shown he should select?
solutionSteps: [1 mark] Correct option: I and III. Ray I (through the optical centre, passing undeviated) and ray III (parallel to the principal axis, refracted through the principal focus) are the two standard correct construction rays for a convex lens. Diagrams II and IV show the refracted ray diverging, which is wrong for a converging lens.

III: a ray parallel to the principal axis refracted so that it passes through the principal focus F beyond the lens. IV: an incident oblique ray emerging parallel to the axis with a dotted diverging extension through F.

runtime_row.subject: Science
runtime_row.questionText: Select from the following the best experimental set-up for tracing the path of a ray of light passing through a rectangular glass slab:
solutionSteps: [1 mark] Correct option: S. For an accurate trace, the two pins fixing the incident ray should be far apart from each other and the angle of incidence should be moderate (roughly 30° to 60°). Only set-up S has both: well-separated pins on a ray at a convenient angle. In P the ray is almost along the normal, and in Q and R the pins are too close together, so small errors in sighting produce large errors in the traced ray.
runtime_row.diagramDescription: Four set-ups P, Q, R, S. Each shows the outline of a rectangular glass slab on paper with a dashed normal at the point of incidence on the top face, and an incident ray marked by two pins (circles) on it. P: ray nearly along the normal, pins moderately spaced. Q: ray at a moderate angle but with the pins spaced close to the slab. R: ray at an angle with the two pins very close together. S: ray at a moderate angle of incidence with the two pins fixed far apart.

solutionSteps: [1 mark] In the trace, mark 1 is the angle between the incident ray and the normal at the top surface (angle i); mark 3 is the angle between the emergent ray and the normal at the bottom surface (angle e); mark 2 is the angle between the refracted ray inside the slab and the normal (angle r); mark 4 is the perpendicular shift between the emergent ray and the extended incident ray (lateral displacement). So i, e, r, displacement correspond to 1, 3, 2, 4.
runtime_row.diagramDescription: A rectangular glass slab. A ray is incident at the top surface, where angle 1 is marked between the incident ray and the dashed normal. Inside the slab, angle 2 is marked between the refracted ray and the same normal. At the bottom surface, angle 3 is marked between the emergent ray and the dashed normal there. Label 4 is a double-headed arrow showing the perpendicular gap between the emergent ray and the dotted straight-line extension of the incident ray (lateral displacement).

At the exit point the angle of emergence is marked between the emergent ray and the dashed normal (correct).

runtime_row.questionText: Study the given ray diagrams and select the correct statement from the following:
options: Device X is a concave mirror and device Y is a convex lens, whose focal lengths are 20 cm and 25 cm respectively.
Device X is a convex lens and device Y is a concave mirror, whose focal lengths are 10 cm and 25 cm respectively.
Device X is a concave lens and device Y is a convex mirror, whose focal lengths are 20 cm and 25 cm respectively.
Device X is a convex lens and device Y is a concave mirror, whose focal lengths are 20 cm and 25 cm respectively.
runtime_row.answer: Device X is a convex lens and device Y is a concave mirror, whose focal lengths are 20 cm and 25 cm respectively.
solutionSteps: [1 mark] Light PASSES THROUGH device X and converges 20 cm beyond it, so X is a convex lens of focal length 20 cm; light is REFLECTED by device Y and converges 25 cm in front of it (same side as the incident light), so Y is a concave mirror of focal length 25 cm.
runtime_row.finalAnswer: Device X is a convex lens and device Y is a concave mirror, whose focal lengths are 20 cm and 25 cm respectively.

Right: parallel rays strike a device Y and converge to a point on a screen placed 25 cm in FRONT of Y, on the same side as the incoming rays (light reflected back by the device).

runtime_row.questionText: A light ray enters from medium A to medium B as shown in Figure 10.2. The refractive index of medium B relative to A will be
solutionSteps: [1 mark] (a) greater than unity — in Fig. 10.2 the ray bends TOWARDS the normal as it enters medium B, which happens only when light goes from a rarer to a denser medium; the angle of refraction is smaller than the angle of incidence, so n(B/A) = sin i / sin r > 1.
runtime_row.strategyHint: REQUIRES-FIGURE: Ray bending TOWARDS the normal when entering medium B from A.

runtime_row.questionText: Beams of light are incident through the holes A and B and emerge out of box through the holes C and D respectively as shown in Figure 10.3. Which of the following could be inside the box?

runtime_row.questionText: Find out, from Table 9.3, the medium having highest optical density. Also find the medium with lowest optical density.

runtime_row.questionText: (a) (i) State laws of reflection of light. (ii) An object of height 5·0 cm is placed at 15 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. At what distance from the mirror should a screen be placed, so that a focussed image is obtained on it ? Find the height of the image. 5 OR (b) (i) State laws of refraction of light. (ii) Draw a ray diagram to show refraction of a ray of light through a rectangular glass slab. How is the emergent ray related to incident ray ? Mark lateral displacement in the diagram. 5 22 >
runtime_row.answer: (a) (i) Laws of reflection. (ii) Screen 30 cm in front of the mirror (v = –30 cm); image height –10 cm (real, inverted, magnified). OR (b) (i) Laws of refraction (Snell's law). (ii) Ray diagram through a rectangular glass slab; the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray, displaced laterally.
solutionSteps: [2 marks] (a) (i) The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection. The incident ray, the normal to the mirror at the point of incidence and the reflected ray, all lie in the same plane. OR (b) (i) The incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal to the interface of two transparent media at the point of incidence, all lie in the same plane. The ratio of sine of angle of incidence to the sine of angle of refraction is a constant, for the light of a given colour and for the given pair of media (Snell's law: sin i / sin r = constant).

[1 mark] (a) (ii) u = – 15 cm, f = −10 cm (concave mirror), h = 5⋅0 cm. Mirror formula 1/f = 1/v + 1/u ⇒ 1/v = 1/f – 1/u = –1/10 + 1/15 = (–3 + 2)/30 = –1/30 ⇒ v = – 30 cm. OR (b) (ii) Ray diagram: a ray incident obliquely on a rectangular glass slab bends towards the normal on entering (angle r) and away from the normal on leaving (angle e = i).

[2 marks] (a) The screen must be placed at a distance of 30 cm from the mirror, in front of it. h′ = –(v/u) × h = –(–30/–15) × 5 = –10 cm: the image is real, inverted and 10 cm high. OR (b) • The emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray. • The perpendicular distance between the incident ray produced and the emergent ray is the lateral displacement, labelled on the diagram.
runtime_row.finalAnswer: (a) (ii) v = –30 cm (screen 30 cm in front), h′ = –10 cm; OR (b) emergent ray parallel to the incident ray, lateral displacement marked

runtime_row.subtopic: Lens / Concave Mirror — Image Position via Formula
runtime_row.questionText:
The image shows a thin lens of focal length 5 m.
(i) What is the kind of lens shown in the above figure?
(ii) If a real inverted image is to be formed by this lens at a distance of 7 m from the optical centre, then show with calculation where should the object be placed?
(iii) Draw a neatly labelled diagram of the image formation mentioned in (ii).

[OR]

A 10 cm long pencil is placed 5 cm in front of a concave mirror having a radius of curvature of 40 cm.
(i) Determine the position of the image formed by this mirror.
(ii) What is the size of the image?
(iii) Draw a ray diagram to show the formation of the image as mentioned in part (i).
runtime_row.answer: Main: (i) Convex lens. (ii) Object at u = −17.5 m (17.5 m on the left). (iii) Diagram with object beyond 2F. OR Alt: (i) Image at v = +6.67 cm behind mirror (virtual). (ii) Image size = (4/3)·10 ≈ 13.33 cm. (iii) Ray diagram with object between pole and focus.
solutionSteps: [1 mark] Main (i): A real inverted image is produced only by a converging lens — hence the lens is a Convex lens.

[1 mark] Main (ii): Lens formula: 1/f = 1/v − 1/u, with f = +5 m and v = +7 m (real image on opposite side). 1/u = 1/v − 1/f = 1/7 − 1/5 = (5 − 7)/35 = −2/35. So u = −35/2 = −17.5 m. Object is placed 17.5 m on the left of the convex lens.

[1 mark] Main (iii): Ray diagram (two rays from object): one ray parallel to principal axis refracts through F on the other side; second ray through optical centre passes undeviated. Both meet to form a real, inverted, diminished image at v = +7 m. Object placed beyond 2F (since |u| = 17.5 > 2f = 10).

[1 mark] OR (alternative i): Mirror formula 1/f = 1/v + 1/u with f = −20 cm (concave, half of R = 40 cm) and u = −5 cm. 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = −1/20 + 1/5 = (−1 + 4)/20 = 3/20. v = 20/3 ≈ +6.67 cm. Positive v → image is behind the mirror, so virtual and erect.

[1 mark] OR (ii–iii): Magnification m = −v/u = −(20/3)/(−5) = 4/3. h₂ = m·h₁ = (4/3)·10 = 13.33 cm — image is enlarged (and erect). Ray diagram: object between pole P and focus F; two rays — one parallel (reflects through F), one through C (reflects back); diverging reflected rays appear to meet behind the mirror, giving virtual, erect, enlarged image.
runtime_row.finalAnswer: Main: (i) Convex lens; (ii) u = −17.5 m; (iii) diagram. OR Alt: (i) v = +6.67 cm; (ii) image size ≈ 13.33 cm; (iii) ray diagram.

runtime_row.questionText:
The image is that of a Digital Single Lens Reflex (DSLR) camera, used to take high-resolution photographs by professional photographers. The second image is a schematic diagram of how an image is formed on the sensor of the camera. Based on your understanding of lenses, answer the following questions.
A. What type of lens is used in the DSLR camera shown in the image?
B. What type of image is formed on the sensor?
Attempt either subpart C or D.
C. A photographer is using a DSLR camera with a lens of focal length f = 50 mm to take a close-up photograph of a small object. The lens projects an image onto the camera sensor that is located 60 mm behind the lens. Calculate the object distance (i.e., the distance between the object and the lens).
OR
D. A photographer is using a DSLR camera to take a picture of a flower. The flower is positioned 150 mm away from the camera lens. The actual height of the flower is 80 mm, and the image height formed on the camera's sensor is measured to be 20 mm (inverted). Calculate the focal length of the camera lens.
runtime_row.answer: A. Convex lens B. Real and inverted C. u = -300 mm (object 300 mm in front of the lens) OR D. f = 30 mm
solutionSteps: [1 mark] A. A CONVEX (converging) lens is used in the DSLR camera.
[1 mark] B. A REAL and INVERTED (and diminished) image is formed on the sensor.

[1 mark] EITHER C (working): with f = +50 mm and v = +60 mm, the lens formula gives 1/u = 1/v - 1/f = 1/60 - 1/50 = -1/300. [OR D (working): m = image height / object height = (-20)/80 = -1/4; since m = v/u, v = m × u = (-1/4) × (-150) = +37.5 mm.]
[1 mark] EITHER C (final answer): u = -300 mm — the object is 300 mm in front of the lens. [OR D (final answer): 1/f = 1/v - 1/u = 1/37.5 + 1/150 = 5/150, so f = 30 mm.]
runtime_row.finalAnswer: A. Convex lens B. Real, inverted C. 300 mm in front of the lens (OR D. f = 30 mm)

runtime_row.subject: Science
runtime_row.question:
A student placed an object 30 cm in front of a convex lens of focal length 20 cm.
(a) Find the position of the image using the lens formula.
(b) What is the magnification?
(c) State the nature of the image (real/virtual, inverted/erect, magnified/diminished).
(d) If the object is moved to a position 15 cm from the lens, how does the image change?
runtime_row.answer: (a) Using 1/v − 1/u = 1/f: 1/v − 1/(−30) = 1/20 ⇒ 1/v = 1/20 − 1/30 = 1/60 ⇒ v = 60 cm. (b) m = v/u = 60/(−30) = −2 (magnification is 2×). (c) Real, inverted, magnified (since |m| > 1). (d) At 15 cm, object is between F and optical centre. Using 1/v − 1/(−15) = 1/20 ⇒ 1/v = 1/20 − 1/15 = −1/60 ⇒ v = −60 cm. Image is virtual, erect, and magnified.
runtime_row.explanation: Case-based optics problem testing lens formula application with different object positions.

runtime_row.questionText: Smriti is looking at herself in a convex mirror in a science museum, standing 2 m away from the mirror. Her image appears to be around half her actual height. Estimate the focal length of the mirror.
runtime_row.answer: f = +2 m (convex mirror of focal length 2 m)
solutionSteps: [½ mark] Identify the object distance: u = -2 m (object in front of the mirror).
[1 mark] The image is half her height, virtual and erect, so m = +1/2. Using m = -v/u: v = -m × u = -(1/2) × (-2 m) = +1 m (image behind the mirror).
[½ mark] Use the correct mirror formula: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f.
[1 mark] 1/f = 1/(+1) + 1/(-2) = 1/2, so f = +2 m. The mirror is convex with focal length 2 m.

runtime_row.subject: Science
runtime_row.questionText:
In a human eye, the distance between the lens and the retina is 17 mm. The light entering the eye gets refracted at the cornea and then at the lens. Ciliary muscles in the eye can control the focal length of the lens by changing its shape.
(a) Diana is looking at the Moon. What is the focal length of the combination of cornea and the lens in Diana's eyes at this time?
(b) Diana is reading a book kept at a distance of 20 cm from her eyes. What is the focal length of the combination of the cornea and the lens in Diana's eyes at this time?
(c) When Diana brings the book closer to her eyes, the letters appear blurry to her and she cannot read the book. Explain why the letters appear blurry to her.
runtime_row.answer: (a) 17 mm (b) approximately 15.7 mm (c) the image forms behind the retina
solutionSteps: [½ mark] (a) The Moon is effectively at infinity, so the image forms at the focus: focal length = distance to the retina = 17 mm.
[½ mark] (b) Substitute into the lens formula 1/f = 1/v - 1/u with v = +17 mm (retina) and u = -200 mm (book 20 cm in front of the eye).
[1 mark] 1/f = 1/17 + 1/200 = 217/3400, so f = 3400/217 which is approximately 15.7 mm (the eye SHORTENS its focal length to focus a nearer object).
[1 mark] (c) The eye lens cannot shorten its focal length beyond a limit (least distance of distinct vision). For a closer book the image forms BEHIND the retina, so the letters appear blurry.
runtime_row.finalAnswer: (a) 17 mm (b) about 15.7 mm (c) image moves behind the retina

runtime_row.subtopic: Ray Diagrams and Lens Formula (Convex Lens)
runtime_row.questionText:
(a) Copy the scaled ray diagram given (a pencil of length 4 cm held horizontally, 2 cm above the principal axis; its pointed end is 5 cm from a thin convex lens of focal length 3 cm). Draw more required incident rays from the pencil to illustrate the formation of the image of the pencil by the convex lens. Your completed diagram should show the image of the whole pencil. (Note: assume the lens is a thin lens.)
(b) What is the distance of the image of the pointed end of the pencil from the lens?
(c) What is the length of the image of the pencil?
runtime_row.answer: (b) 7.5 cm from the lens (c) about 3.6 cm
solutionSteps: [1 mark] (a) Draw one more correctly drawn incident ray from the pointed end of the pencil (e.g. through the optical centre, undeviated).
[2 marks] (a) Draw two correctly drawn rays from the blunt/rear end (parallel-to-axis ray refracting through F, and the ray through the optical centre) to locate its image point.

[1 mark] (a) Join the two image points to show the image of the WHOLE pencil (it comes out inverted, magnified and tilted). Check by lens formula: pointed end u = -5 cm, 1/v = 1/3 - 1/5 = 2/15 so v = +7.5 cm with m = v/u = -1.5 (image height 3 cm below axis); rear end u = -9 cm, 1/v = 1/3 - 1/9 = 2/9 so v = +4.5 cm with m = -0.5 (image height 1 cm below axis).
[½ mark] (b) The image of the pointed end is 7.5 cm from the lens (on the far side).
[½ mark] (c) Image length = distance between the two image points = sqrt((7.5 - 4.5)^2 + (3 - 1)^2) = sqrt(13) which is approximately 3.6 cm.
runtime_row.diagramDescription: Scaled ray diagram: a horizontal pencil 4 cm long, 2 cm above the principal axis, its tip 5 cm in front of a thin convex lens (f = 3 cm); one ray from the tip through the optical centre is already drawn.

runtime_row.subject: Science
runtime_row.questionText: The image shows the refraction of light in three transparent rectangular blocks X, Y and Z, made of different materials, when they are placed in air. The angle of incidence is different in each case (i3 > i2 > i1) but the angle of refraction r is the same in all three blocks. Compare the speed of light in the three blocks. Justify your answer.
runtime_row.answer: Speed in X > speed in Y > speed in Z.
solutionSteps: [1 mark] Speed of light: speed in X > speed in Y > speed in Z.
[½ mark] By Snell's law n = sin i / sin r with r the same for all three: the angle of incidence is smallest for X (i1), so the refractive index of X is the smallest (and Z's is the largest).
[½ mark] Since n = c/v, a smaller refractive index means a larger speed - so light is fastest in X and slowest in Z.
runtime_row.diagramDescription: Three rectangular blocks X, Y, Z each with an incident ray (angles i1, i2, i3 where i3 > i2 > i1) refracting to the SAME angle r inside the block.

runtime_row.subject: Science
runtime_row.questionText:
State the type of mirror preferred as
(i) rear view mirrors in vehicles
(ii) shaving mirrors.
Justify your answer giving two reasons in each case.
solutionSteps: [½ mark] (i) Convex mirror is preferred as a rear view mirror.
[1 mark] Reasons: it always forms an erect (though diminished) image of the traffic behind, and it gives a much wider field of view than a plane mirror of the same size.
[½ mark] (ii) Concave mirror is preferred as a shaving mirror.
[1 mark] Reasons: when the face is held between the pole and the principal focus it forms an erect, magnified image, and the enlarged, well-lit view makes a closer, smoother shave possible.
runtime_row.finalAnswer: (i) Convex - erect image + wide field of view; (ii) Concave - erect, magnified image when the face is within the focus.

runtime_row.questionText:
The image (see figure) shows the formation of an image with an optical instrument, shown schematically as a rectangle: an object arrow 20 cm from the instrument forms a smaller upright image 10 cm from it, on the same side.
A. Identify the optical instrument in the image.
B. What type of image is formed in this case?
C. Based on the measurements given in the image, calculate the focal length of the instrument.
runtime_row.answer: A. Concave lens B. Virtual, erect and diminished C. f = -20 cm
solutionSteps: [½ mark] A. The instrument is a CONCAVE lens (the emergent rays diverge and the image is upright, smaller and on the object's side).
[½ mark] B. The image formed is VIRTUAL (erect and diminished).
[1 mark] C. With u = -20 cm and v = -10 cm, the lens formula 1/f = 1/v - 1/u = -1/10 + 1/20 = -1/20 gives f = -20 cm (negative, as expected for a concave lens).
runtime_row.finalAnswer: Concave lens; virtual image; f = -20 cm

runtime_row.subject: Science
runtime_row.questionText: A straight vertical copper wire passes through the centre O of a horizontal cardboard ABCD and is connected to a battery through a plug key (NCERT Exemplar Figure 13.1). If the key is taken out (the circuit is made open) and magnetic field lines are drawn over the horizontal plane ABCD, the lines are
options: straight lines parallel to each other
concentric circles near the point O but of elliptical shapes as we go away from it
runtime_row.answer: straight lines parallel to each other
solutionSteps: With the key open no current flows in the wire, so the wire produces no magnetic field; only the Earth's (nearly uniform) magnetic field acts on the plane ABCD, whose field lines are straight lines parallel to each other → option (c).

runtime_row.subject: Science
runtime_row.questionText: A uniform magnetic field exists in the plane of paper pointing from left to right as shown in Figure 13.3. In the field an electron and a proton move as shown. The electron and the proton experience
options: forces both pointing into the plane of paper
forces both pointing out of the plane of paper
forces pointing into the plane of paper and out of the plane of paper, respectively
force pointing opposite and along the direction of the uniform magnetic field respectively
runtime_row.answer: forces both pointing into the plane of paper
solutionSteps: Force on a moving charge: F = q v × B. Note the sign of charge.
The proton (positive) and the electron (negative) move in opposite directions in the figure, but the negative sign of the electron's charge flips the cross-product direction.
Working out v × B and multiplying by the respective sign of charge gives the same force direction for both — both INTO the plane of paper.
Hence option (a) is correct.
runtime_row.finalAnswer: Option (a): both forces point into the plane of paper.
runtime_row.strategyHint: REQUIRES-FIGURE: B field arrows left→right; electron and proton velocities as shown. Use F = qv × B with sign of charge.

runtime_row.subject: Science
runtime_row.questionText: (A) (i) Draw a diagram showing the magnetic field lines around a bar magnet. Write any two characteristics of magnetic field lines. (ii) Write the statement of Right hand thumb rule. (iii) The concentric circles representing the magnetic field around a current carrying straight wire become larger and larger as we move away from the wire. How does magnetic field change on these concentric circles ? OR (B) (i) Draw a diagram, showing the magnetic field lines in and around the current carrying solenoid. Write any two salient features of these lines. (ii) What is an electromagnet and how is it made ? ____________ of 32 1191-1
solutionSteps: (A) (i) Characteristics: • The magnet field lines emerge from north pole and merge at south pole.
Inside the magnet, the direction of field lines is from its south pole to its north pole.

Thus, the magnetic field lines are closed curves. • The relative strength of the magnetic field is shown by the degree of closeness of the field lines. 1 PAGE10 (SET 31/5/1) • No two fieldlines are found to cross each other.
(any two) (ii) Imagine that you are holding a current carrying straight conductor in your right hand such that the thumb points towards the direction of current.
Then your fingers will wrap around the conductor in the direction of field lines of the magnetic field.
(iii) As the concentric circles become larger and larger, the magnetic field decreases.
OR (B) (i) Salient features: • The pattern of the magnetic field lines in a solenoid is similar to that of a bar magnet. • Field lines inside the solenoid are in the form of parallel straight lines.

(ii) • A magnetic material which behaves like a magnet on passing electric current through it is called an electromagnet. • It is made by wrapping a current carrying insulated copper wire in the form of a coil around a magnetic material like soft iron / By placing a magnetic material like soft iron as a core material inside the current carrying solenoid.

runtime_row.subtopic: Magnetic Field due to Circular Loop
runtime_row.questionText: A circular loop placed in a plane perpendicular to the plane of paper carries a current when the key is ON. The current as seen from points A and B (in the plane of paper and on the axis of the coil) is anti-clockwise and clockwise respectively. The magnetic field lines point from B to A. The N-pole of the resultant magnet is on the face close to
options: A if the current is small, and B if the current is large
B if the current is small and A if the current is large
solutionSteps: Apply the right-hand thumb rule for a circular current loop: curl the fingers along the direction of current and the thumb gives the direction of the magnetic field (and the N-pole).
As seen from A, current is anti-clockwise — so curling the right-hand fingers anti-clockwise (when looking from A) makes the thumb point OUT towards A.
Hence on the face near A, magnetic field emerges → this face acts as the N-pole.
This is consistent with the field lines pointing from B to A externally (S to N inside, N to S outside is the convention).

runtime_row.questionText: A helical coil whose length is greater than its diameter is connected to a battery (as shown). (a) How does the magnetic field at point P compare with the magnetic field at point Q? Justify your answer. (b) State one way in which the strength of the magnetic field inside a current carrying helical coil can be changed.
runtime_row.answer: (a) Same at P and Q (uniform field inside solenoid). (b) Change number of turns or current.
solutionSteps: (a) The helical coil acts as a solenoid. Inside a solenoid (length >> diameter), the magnetic field is UNIFORM and consists of parallel straight lines. So magnetic field at P = magnetic field at Q.
(b) To change the strength: (i) increase/decrease the number of turns per unit length, OR (ii) increase/decrease the current through the coil. (Also: insert an iron core to dramatically increase B.)

runtime_row.questionText: (a) Describe an activity to determine the direction of magnetic field produced by a current carrying straight conductor. Also show that the direction of the magnetic field is reversed on reversing the direction of current. (b) An a -particle, (which is a positively charged particle) benters, a uniform magnetic field at right angles to it as shown below. Stating the relevant principle explain in which direction will this a-particle moves?
runtime_row.answer: (a) Fix a cardboard and pass a straight wire through a hole in cardboard and connect the two ends of the wire with a cell through a rheostat and key with a cell. Sprinkle iron filings uniformly on the card board. Pass the current in the wire and gently tap the card board. You wou
solutionSteps: [1 mark] (a) Activity set-up: pass a straight copper wire vertically through a hole in a horizontal cardboard; connect its ends to a cell through a key and a rheostat. Sprinkle iron filings uniformly on the cardboard.

[1 mark] Pass the current and gently tap the cardboard: the iron filings align themselves in concentric circles around the wire — these represent the magnetic field lines around a straight current-carrying conductor. Placing a small compass at a point shows the direction of the field along these circles (given by the right-hand thumb rule).
[1 mark] On reversing the direction of current, the compass needle deflects in the opposite way — the direction of the magnetic field is reversed.

[1 mark] (b) Relevant principle — Fleming's left-hand rule: stretch the forefinger, middle finger and thumb of the left hand mutually perpendicular; the forefinger gives the field direction, the middle finger the current direction, and the thumb the force (motion).

[1 mark] The moving positive α-particle is equivalent to a conventional current in its direction of motion; applying Fleming's left-hand rule with the field at right angles, the α-particle experiences a force perpendicular to both and is deflected in the direction given by the thumb (upwards in the shown figure).

runtime_row.subject: Science
runtime_row.question: Rohan’s bicycle rusts quickly in a coastal area. Suggest two methods to prevent rusting and briefly explain why each method works.
runtime_row.answer: Painting and applying oil/grease or galvanising.
runtime_row.explanation: Painting and oil/grease create a protective layer, preventing oxygen and water from reaching the iron surface. Galvanising coats iron with zinc which is more reactive and protects by sacrificial action.
solutionSteps: Method 1: Painting the bicycle.; Painting creates a physical barrier, preventing the iron surface from coming into contact with oxygen and moisture, which are necessary for rusting. [1]
Method 2: Galvanising the bicycle parts. [1]
Galvanising involves coating the iron with a layer of zinc. [1]
Zinc is more reactive than iron, so it corrodes preferentially, protecting the iron even if the coating is scratched (sacrificial protection). [1]
runtime_row.finalAnswer: Painting and applying oil/grease or galvanising.

runtime_row.subject: Science
runtime_row.questionText:
A piece of iron rusts when it comes in contact with air and moisture. Prakash had two identical shiny iron pieces P and Q. To prevent the pieces from rusting, he coated piece P with oil paint and he galvanized piece Q with a coat of zinc metal. He noticed that the coatings were not complete and that a small part of the iron was exposed in both the pieces.

What is Prakash likely to observe about the exposed parts of the two iron pieces after some days? Explain why.
runtime_row.answer: The exposed part of piece P is rusted; the exposed part of piece Q is not rusted. Oil painting prevents rusting only by preventing contact of iron with moist air, whereas galvanising also protects by zinc getting oxidised in preference to iron as it is more reactive than iron.
solutionSteps: [2 marks] 1 mark each for the following: The exposed part of piece P is rusted. The exposed part of piece Q not rusted.

[2 marks] 1 mark each for the following: Oil painting prevents rusting only by preventing contact of iron with moist air. [1 mark] Galvanising also protects by zinc getting oxidised in preference to iron as it is more reactive than iron. [1 mark]
runtime_row.finalAnswer: P's exposed part rusts, Q's does not - paint is only a physical barrier, while zinc gives sacrificial protection.

runtime_row.subject: Science
runtime_row.questionText:
A car manufacturer uses three different methods to prevent corrosion of car parts:
Method 1: Painting with thick protective coating
Method 2: Galvanization with zinc layer
Method 3: Using stainless steel (iron with chromium and nickel)
Explain how each method prevents corrosion and identify which method is most effective for long-term protection.
runtime_row.answer: Method 3 (stainless steel) is most effective due to passive chromium oxide layer
solutionSteps: Method 1 (Painting): Creates physical barrier preventing oxygen and moisture contact
Method 2 (Galvanization): Zinc is more reactive, gets oxidized first, sacrifices itself
Method 3 (Stainless steel): Chromium forms thin, transparent, self-healing oxide layer (passive film)
Method 3 is most effective because: passive layer is self-repairing, doesn't require maintenance
Methods 1 & 2 can wear off or be damaged over time
runtime_row.finalAnswer: Method 3 (stainless steel) is most effective due to passive chromium oxide layer

runtime_row.subject: Science
runtime_row.questionText:
A student observes that when copper turnings are heated with oxygen, they turn black. When hydrogen gas is passed over the black powder, it turns red again and water is produced.

A) What is the black powder formed? Write its chemical formula.
B) Name the type of reaction in both processes.
C) Why does the black powder turn red when hydrogen is passed over it?
D) What is the principle used in this reaction?
runtime_row.answer: A) CuO (Copper oxide), B) Oxidation and Reduction, C) Hydrogen is a reducing agent, D) Displacement principle
solutionSteps: A) When Cu is heated with O₂: 2Cu + O₂ → 2CuO (black powder)
B) First process is oxidation (Cu loses electrons), second is reduction (O is removed)
C) H₂ + CuO → Cu + H₂O (Hydrogen reduces copper oxide, restoring red color)
D) This demonstrates the principle that more reactive elements can displace less reactive ones
runtime_row.finalAnswer: A) CuO (Copper oxide), B) Oxidation and Reduction, C) Hydrogen is a reducing agent, D) Displacement principle

runtime_row.answer: (any two) (b) 100 J • Autotrophs ⎯⎯⎯ →Primary consumer ⎯⎯⎯→ secondary 10000 J (1000 J) consumer (100 J)
solutionSteps: a) • The energy captured by plants does not revert to solar input and the energy which passes to the herbivores does not revert back to autotrophs. • As energy moves progressively through the various trophic levels
it is no longer available to the previous level. • The energy available at each trophic level gets diminished progressively due to loss of energy at each level.
(any two) (b) 100 J • Autotrophs ⎯⎯⎯ →Primary consumer ⎯⎯⎯→ secondary 10000 J (1000 J) consumer (100 J)
runtime_row.finalAnswer: (any two) (b) 100 J • Autotrophs ⎯⎯⎯ →Primary consumer ⎯⎯⎯→ secondary 10000 J (1000 J) consumer (100 J)

runtime_row.subject: Science
runtime_row.questionText: In periods of high rainfall, fertiliser can flow into lake ecosystems. Explain what is meant by the term ecosystem.
runtime_row.answer: An ecosystem is a community of organisms (plants and animals) living together in a habitat, which interact with one another (biotic factors) and with their non-living surroundings (abiotic factors such as climate, water, light).
solutionSteps: [1 mark] An ecosystem includes the living organisms - the plants and animals.
[1 mark] These organisms live together in a habitat / community.
[1 mark] The organisms interact with each other (biotic interactions).
[1 mark] The organisms also interact with their non-living surroundings (abiotic factors, e.g. climate, water, light).
runtime_row.finalAnswer: An ecosystem is a community of organisms in a habitat interacting with each other (biotic) and with their non-living surroundings (abiotic).

runtime_row.subject: Science
runtime_row.subtopic: Effect of Pesticide on a Food Chain and Bioaccumulation
runtime_row.questionText: A farmer sprays their spinach with pesticide and kills most of the caterpillars, though some caterpillars survive. The food chain is spinach → caterpillar → blackbird → eagle. Discuss the impact on the food chain.
runtime_row.answer: With fewer caterpillars there is less food for the blackbirds, so blackbird numbers fall / they die out; this means less food for the eagles, so eagle numbers fall / they die out. The pesticide in the surviving caterpillars transfers to the consumers that eat them and bioaccumulates up the chain in the blackbirds and eagles.
solutionSteps: [1 mark] Killing most caterpillars leaves less food for the blackbirds, so blackbird numbers fall / they may die out.
[1 mark] With fewer blackbirds there is less food for the eagles, so eagle numbers fall / they may die out.
[1 mark] Pesticide in the surviving caterpillars is transferred to the consumers (blackbirds, then eagles) when they are eaten.
[1 mark] The pesticide bioaccumulates, building up to higher concentrations in consumers higher up the chain (eagles), which can harm them.
runtime_row.finalAnswer: Fewer caterpillars mean less food up the chain (blackbirds then eagles decline), and pesticide in surviving caterpillars bioaccumulates in the consumers, harming the top predators.

runtime_row.subject: Science
runtime_row.questionText: Detergents are non-biodegradable. Explain two negative environmental impacts of detergents in a lake ecosystem.
runtime_row.answer: Detergents contain phosphates that act as fertiliser, causing algal blooms; subsequent decomposition causes eutrophication and oxygen depletion, leading to death of aquatic organisms.
solutionSteps: [1 mark] Detergents act as a fertiliser because they contain phosphates.
[1 mark] This causes increased growth of algae / an algal bloom.
[1 mark] Decomposition of algae by microbes increases respiration, causing eutrophication / oxygen depletion in the water.
[1 mark] Oxygen depletion (and endocrine disruption of aquatic animals) leads to death of fish, plants and other organisms.
runtime_row.finalAnswer: Phosphates cause algal bloom; resulting eutrophication / oxygen depletion kills aquatic organisms.

runtime_row.subject: Science
runtime_row.questionText: Distinguish between a food chain and a food web, giving one example of each. Explain, using the idea of energy transfer between trophic levels, why a food chain in nature rarely has more than four or five links.
runtime_row.answer: A food chain is a single linear feeding pathway (e.g. Grass -> Deer -> Tiger); a food web is many interlinked food chains. Because only about 10% of energy passes to each next level, the usable energy runs out after four or five levels, so chains stay short.
solutionSteps: [1 mark] Food chain: a single, straight-line sequence of organisms through which energy and nutrients pass, each organism eating the one before it. Each stage is a trophic level. Example: Grass -> Deer -> Tiger.

[1 mark] Food web: a network formed by many food chains that are interconnected, because most organisms eat, and are eaten by, more than one kind of organism. Example: in a grassland the grass is eaten by deer, rabbits and grasshoppers, which are in turn eaten by several predators, so the chains cross and link.

[1 mark] Key differences: a food chain is a single isolated pathway and is less stable, whereas a food web offers alternative food routes and so makes the ecosystem more stable; if one species is lost, a web can adjust but a lone chain may break.

[1 mark] Energy transfer: at each trophic level only about 10% of the energy is stored as body mass and passed to the next level (the ten per cent law); about 90% is lost as heat in respiration and other life processes.

[1 mark] Consequence for chain length: because the energy left keeps falling to a tenth at each step, after four or five levels the energy remaining is too little to support a further trophic level, so food chains in nature are usually limited to three to five links.
runtime_row.finalAnswer: A food chain is one linear pathway while a food web is interlinked chains; because ~10% energy transfers per level, energy is exhausted after 4-5 levels, keeping food chains short.

Arrows point in the direction of energy flow (from eaten to eater), showing several chains crossing to form a web. Alongside, a simple linear food chain Grass -> Deer -> Tiger for contrast.

runtime_row.subject: Science
runtime_row.questionText: A food chain in a grassland is: Grass -> Grasshopper -> Lizard -> Snake -> Hawk. The grass (producer) traps 1,00,000 J of energy. Using the ten per cent law, calculate the energy available at each successive trophic level, name the trophic level occupied by each organism, and state one conclusion about the length of food chains that follows from your figures.
runtime_row.answer: Using the ten per cent law: Grass (T1) = 1,00,000 J, Grasshopper (T2) = 10,000 J, Lizard (T3) = 1,000 J, Snake (T4) = 100 J, Hawk (T5) = 10 J. The energy falls to only 10 J at the fifth level, showing why food chains rarely exceed four or five links.
solutionSteps: [1 mark] Ten per cent law: only about 10% of the energy present at one trophic level is stored as body mass and handed on to the next level; the remaining ~90% is lost mainly as heat in respiration and life activities.

[1 mark] Naming the trophic levels: Grass = producer (T1); Grasshopper = primary consumer / herbivore (T2); Lizard = secondary consumer (T3); Snake = tertiary consumer (T4); Hawk = quaternary consumer / top carnivore (T5).
[1 mark] Energy at the lower levels: T1 grass = 1,00,000 J; T2 grasshopper = 10% of 1,00,000 = 10,000 J; T3 lizard = 10% of 10,000 = 1,000 J.
[1 mark] Energy at the higher levels: T4 snake = 10% of 1,000 = 100 J; T5 hawk = 10% of 100 = 10 J.

[1 mark] Conclusion: the energy has fallen from 1,00,000 J to just 10 J - only one ten-thousandth of the producer energy - by the fifth level. So little energy is left that a further trophic level could not be supported, which is why food chains are usually limited to four or five levels.
runtime_row.finalAnswer: T1 = 1,00,000 J, T2 = 10,000 J, T3 = 1,000 J, T4 = 100 J, T5 = 10 J; the rapid ten-fold drop per level leaves too little energy after 4-5 links, so food chains stay short.
runtime_row.diagramDescription: A horizontal food chain illustrating the ten per cent law: Grass (T1, 1,00,000 J) -> Grasshopper (T2, 10,000 J) -> Lizard (T3, 1,000 J) -> Snake (T4, 100 J) -> Hawk (T5, 10 J). Each arrow is labelled to show that only about 10% of the energy passes to the next level while about 90% is lost as heat and in respiration, so the energy available decreases ten-fold along the chain.

runtime_row.subject: Maths
runtime_row.questionText: A rectangular garden has perimeter 56 meters. If the length is increased by 2 meters and width is decreased by 2 meters, the perimeter remains the same. Find (a) the linear equations, (b) the original dimensions.
runtime_row.answer: The equations are dependent; infinitely many solutions exist where l + w = 28
solutionSteps: Let length = l, width = w
(a) Original perimeter: 2(l + w) = 56, so l + w = 28
New perimeter: 2(l + 2 + w - 2) = 2(l + w) = 56
Both equations give l + w = 28
These are the same equation (coincident lines)
(b) Infinitely many solutions possible
Any l and w such that l + w = 28 satisfies both conditions
runtime_row.finalAnswer: The equations are dependent; infinitely many solutions exist where l + w = 28

Aman bought 3 pens and 2 pencils for Rs 60. Beena bought 2 pens and 5 pencils for Rs 65.
(a) Form a pair of linear equations.
(b) Solve for the cost of a pen and a pencil.
(c) What is the cost of 4 pens and 4 pencils?
runtime_row.answer: (a) Let cost of pen = x, pencil = y. Equations: 3x + 2y = 60 and 2x + 5y = 65. (b) Multiply eq1 by 5 and eq2 by 2: 15x + 10y = 300, 4x + 10y = 130. Subtracting: 11x = 170 ⇒ x = 170/11 ≈ Rs 15.45. Substituting: y = (60 − 3×170/11)/2 = (660 − 510)/(22) = 150/22 ≈ Rs 6.82. (c) Cost of 4 pens + 4 pencils = 4(15.45 + 6.82) ≈ Rs 89.09.

runtime_row.questionText:
Shown below are the parts of graphs of two polynomials, g(x) and h(x). When h(x) is divided by (x - 3), the remainder is k.

Which of these is true for the remainder when g(x) is divided by (x - 3)?
solutionSteps: [1 mark] Correct option: (1) It is less than k. By the remainder theorem the remainder on dividing by (x - 3) is the value of the polynomial at x = 3, so the two remainders are g(3) and h(3) = k. Both curves pass through the same two x-intercepts, -2 and 2, but h(x) is the narrower, steeper curve, so to the right of x = 2 it has already climbed above g(x). At x = 3 the h(x) curve is therefore higher, giving g(3) < h(3) = k.

runtime_row.questionText:
f(x) = 2x² - 4x + k, where k is a non-zero real number. When f(x) is divided by (x + 2), it leaves a remainder of (-14).

i) Find the zeroes of f(x).
ii) Shown below is the graph of f(x). The vertex is the minimum value of f(x) and the dotted line drawn through the vertex is the axis of symmetry of the graph.

At what point does the axis of symmetry intersect the x-axis? Find the minimum value of f(x).

Show your steps.
runtime_row.answer: i) The zeroes are -3 and 5. ii) The axis of symmetry meets the x-axis at (1, 0), and the minimum value of f(x) is -32.
solutionSteps: [0.5 mark] i) Writes that, since the remainder of f(x)/(x + 2) is -14, therefore f(-2) = -14.
[1 mark] Uses the above step to write the equation as 2(-2)² - 4(-2) + k = -14 and finds the value of k as -30.
[1.5 marks] Factorises f(x) as (2x + 6)(x - 5) and finds the zeroes as -3 and 5.
[1 mark] ii) Finds the point at which the axis of symmetry intersects the x-axis as the average of the two zeroes: (-3 + 5)/2 = 1.
[1 mark] Finds the minimum value of f(x) as f(1) = 2(1)² - 4(1) - 30 = -32.
runtime_row.finalAnswer: Zeroes -3 and 5; the axis of symmetry meets the x-axis at x = 1; the minimum value is -32.

runtime_row.questionText: While playing badminton Ravi has set the barrier chain hung between two posts at the edge of the walkway of a street. It is hung in the shape of a parabola. Based on the above information answer the following questions : (a) Which type of the polynomial (linear, quadratic, cubic etc.) is graphically represented by a parabola ? (b) If the polynomial represented by a parabola, intersects the xaxis at –2 and 3 and yaxis at –3, then write the zeroes of the parabola. (c) Find the expression for the above polynomial. OR (c) If the zeroes of the polynomial are –5 and 3, find its expression.
runtime_row.answer: (a) Quadratic (b) −2 and 3 (c) p(x) = k(x + 2)(x − 3) = k(x² − x − 6); y-intercept −3 ⇒ −6k = −3 ⇒ k = 1/2, so p(x) = (1/2)(x² − x − 6) OR (c) g(x) = (x + 5)(x − 3) = x² + 2x − 15
solutionSteps: [1 mark] (a) A parabola graphically represents a quadratic polynomial.
[1 mark] (b) The zeroes are the x-coordinates of the points where the parabola meets the x-axis, i.e. –2 and 3.
[1 mark] (c) With zeroes –2 and 3: p(x) = k(x + 2)(x – 3) = k(x² – x – 6), k ≠ 0.
[1 mark] It meets the y-axis at –3: p(0) = –6k = –3 ⇒ k = 1/2, so p(x) = (1/2)(x² – x – 6). [OR (c) With zeroes –5 and 3: g(x) = (x + 5)(x – 3) = x² + 2x – 15.]
runtime_row.finalAnswer: (a) Quadratic; (b) zeroes are –2 and 3; (c) p(x) = (1/2)(x² – x – 6) [OR g(x) = x² + 2x – 15].

solutionSteps: [1 mark] (i) Point A lies on the y-axis, so x = 0: p(0) = 136. Coordinates of A = (0, 136).
[1 mark] (ii) Span of the arch = distance between the two x-intercepts = 238.5 + 228.5 = 467 units.

[1 mark] Verification: −(coefficient of x)/(coefficient of x²) = −(−0.025)/(−0.0025) = −10 = sum of zeroes — relationship verified. [OR (iii)(b) p(100) = −0.0025(100)² − 0.025(100) + 136 = −25 − 2.5 + 136 = 108.5; p(−100) = −25 + 2.5 + 136 = 113.5. Since 108.5 ≠ 113.5, p(100) ≠ p(−100) — they are not the same.]

runtime_row.questionText:
Assertion (A): The probability of an event always lies between 0 and 1.
Reason (R): The number of favourable outcomes for an event cannot exceed the total number of equally likely outcomes.
runtime_row.answer: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
runtime_row.explanation: An event's probability is a ratio of non-negative counts to total outcomes and therefore cannot exceed 1. The reason explains why the ratio is bounded.
solutionSteps: Assertion (A) states that probability is between 0 and 1, which is a fundamental property of probability.
Reason (R) states that favourable outcomes cannot exceed total outcomes, which is true by definition of an event.
Since P(E) = (favourable outcomes) / (total outcomes), and favourable outcomes <= total outcomes, it implies 0 <= P(E) <= 1. Thus, R correctly explains A.
runtime_row.finalAnswer: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.

runtime_row.questionText: Manu and Aiza are competing in a 60 km cycling race. Aiza's average speed is 10 km/hr greater than Manu's average speed and she finished the race in 1/2 hour less than Manu. Find the time taken by Manu to finish the race. OR Shown below is a cuboid with water in two different orientations. The length, breadth and height of the cuboid are distinct. The cuboid has 480 cm^3 of water. If the height of water in orientation II is half of that in orientation I, then find the heights of water in both orientations.
runtime_row.answer: Manu took 2 hours. [OR] Orientation I: 12 cm; Orientation II: 6 cm.
solutionSteps: Let Manu's time = t hours, so Manu's speed = 60/t km/hr. Aiza's speed = 60/t + 10 and Aiza's time = t − 1/2.
Multiply by t: 10t^2 − 5t − 30 = 0 ⟹ 2t^2 − t − 6 = 0.
Factorise: (t − 2)(2t + 3) = 0 ⟹ t = 2 (reject t = −3/2).
Manu took 2 hours.

[OR] Let cuboid vertical length in orientation I = h cm; height of water = (h − 4) cm. In orientation II, water height = (h − 4)/2. Volume in II: 5 × h × (h−4)/2 = 480 ⟹ h^2 − 4h − 192 = 0 ⟹ (h − 16)(h + 12) = 0 ⟹ h = 16. Heights: I = 12 cm, II = 6 cm.
runtime_row.finalAnswer: Manu took 2 hours. [OR] I: 12 cm, II: 6 cm.

runtime_row.subject: Maths
runtime_row.questionText: A garden designer is planning a rectangular lawn that is to be surrounded by a uniform walkway. The total area of the lawn and the walkway is 360 square metres. The width of the walkway is same on all sides. The dimensions of the lawn itself are 12 metres by 10 metres. Based on the information given above, answer the following questions : (i) Formulate the quadratic equation representing the total area of the lawn and the walkway, taking width of walkway = x m. 1 (ii) (a) Solve the quadratic equation to find the width of the 2 OR (b) If the cost of paving the walkway at the rate of 50 per square metre is 12,000, calculate the area of the walkway. 2 (iii) Find the perimeter of the lawn. 1
runtime_row.answer: (i) (12 + 2x)(10 + 2x) = 360 ⟹ x² + 11x − 60 = 0 (ii) (a) (x + 15)(x − 4) = 0 ⟹ x = 4; width of the walkway = 4 m OR (b) Area of the walkway = 12000/50 = 240 m² (iii) Perimeter of the lawn = 2(12 + 10) = 44 m
solutionSteps: [1 mark] (i) With walkway width x m, the outer rectangle is (12 + 2x) by (10 + 2x): (12 + 2x)(10 + 2x) = 360 ⟹ 4x² + 44x − 240 = 0 ⟹ x² + 11x − 60 = 0.
[1 mark] (ii)(a) Factorise: (x + 15)(x − 4) = 0 ⟹ x = 4 (reject x = −15 as width cannot be negative).
[1 mark] (ii)(a) Width of the walkway = 4 m. [OR (b) Area of walkway = 12000 ÷ 50 = 240 m².]
[1 mark] (iii) Perimeter of the lawn = 2(12 + 10) = 44 m.
runtime_row.finalAnswer: (i) x² + 11x − 60 = 0; (ii) width = 4 m OR area of walkway = 240 m²; (iii) perimeter of lawn = 44 m.

runtime_row.questionText:
In the centre of a rectangular lawn of dimensions 50 m × 40 m, a rectangular pond is to be constructed so that the area of the grass surrounding the pond is 1184 m². The pond is centred, leaving a uniform border of grass of width w m all around it.
(i) Set up a quadratic equation in w using the given areas.
(ii) Solve to find the dimensions of the pond.
runtime_row.answer: (i) (50 − 2w)(40 − 2w) = 816, i.e. 4w² − 180w + 1184 = 0 (equivalently w² − 45w + 296 = 0). (ii) w = 8 m, so the pond is 34 m × 24 m.
solutionSteps: Total lawn area = 50 × 40 = 2000 m². Grass area = 1184 m² ⇒ pond area = 2000 − 1184 = 816 m².
w = 37 is rejected since 2w must be less than 40. So w = 8 m and the pond is (50 − 16) × (40 − 16) = 34 m × 24 m. Check: 34 × 24 = 816 ✓.
runtime_row.finalAnswer: Quadratic: w² − 45w + 296 = 0; w = 8 m; pond = 34 m × 24 m.
runtime_row.strategyHint: Subtract pond area from lawn area to use the grass-area constraint.

runtime_row.subject: Maths
runtime_row.questionText: Which of the following is NOT a quadratic equation?
solutionSteps: (a): 2(x² − 2x + 1) = 4x² − 2x + 1 ⇒ 2x² + 2x − 1 = 0 — quadratic.
(b): 2x − x² = x² + 5 ⇒ 2x² − 2x + 5 = 0 — quadratic.
(c): (√2 x + √3)² + x² = 2x² + 2√6 x + 3 + x² = 3x² + 2√6 x + 3. Setting equal to 3x² − 5x ⇒ (2√6 + 5)x + 3 = 0 — linear, NOT quadratic.
(d): x⁴ + 4x³ + 4x² = x⁴ + 4x³ + 3 ⇒ 4x² − 3 = 0 — quadratic.
Hence the equation that is NOT quadratic is option (c).
runtime_row.strategyHint: An equation is 'not quadratic' if its given form is not ax² + bx + c = 0 with a ≠ 0.

runtime_row.subject: Maths
runtime_row.questionText: Which of the following is a quadratic equation?
solutionSteps: Expand (x + 1)² = x² + 2x + 1 and RHS = 2x − 6.
Bring all terms to one side: x² + 2x + 1 − 2x + 6 = 0 ⇒ x² + 7 = 0.
This is of the form ax² + bx + c = 0 with a = 1 ≠ 0 — a quadratic equation.
Option (b): x² + x + 8 = x² − 4 ⇒ x + 12 = 0 (linear). Option (c): x² − 4x + 5 = x² − 3x ⇒ −x + 5 = 0 (linear). Option (d): 2x² + 3x = 2x² + 5 ⇒ 3x − 5 = 0 (linear). Only (a) is quadratic.
runtime_row.strategyHint: Expand both sides and check whether the x² coefficient survives — if a = 0 after simplification, it is NOT quadratic.

runtime_row.questionText: For the equation x² - 2(p+1)x + p² = 0, if sum of roots equals product of roots, find p.
solutionSteps: Sum of roots = 2(p+1); Product of roots = p²
Given: Sum = Product ⇒ 2(p + 1) = p² ⇒ p² - 2p - 2 = 0
For real roots, D = 4(p+1)² - 4p² = 4(2p + 1) ≥ 0 ⇒ p ≥ -1/2
p = 1 - √3 ≈ -0.73 < -1/2 gives no real roots, so it is rejected
Hence p = 1 + √3

runtime_row.questionText: Kapoor Travel Agency has sent an AC bus and a minibus with passengers on a trip to Shimla. The AC bus travels at x km/hr while the minibus travels at a speed of 10 km/hr more than the AC bus. The AC bus took 2 hrs more than the minibus in covering 600 km. What is the speed of the AC bus?
solutionSteps: [1 mark] Express the condition: speed of minibus = (x + 10) km/hr; AC bus time − minibus time = 2, i.e. 600/x − 600/(x + 10) = 2.
[1 mark] Frame the quadratic equation: 600(x + 10) − 600x = 2x(x + 10) → 6000 = 2x² + 20x → x² + 10x − 3000 = 0.
[1 mark] x = 50 or x = −60; reject the negative value, so the speed of the AC bus = 50 km/hr.

A school is planning to distribute prizes. They have 240 pens and 168 notebooks. They want to distribute them in equal groups such that each group has the same number of pens and notebooks.
(a) Find the HCF of 240 and 168 using prime factorisation.
(b) How many groups can be formed?
(c) How many pens and notebooks will each group receive?
runtime_row.answer: (a) 240 = 2⁴ × 3 × 5, 168 = 2³ × 3 × 7. HCF = 2³ × 3 = 24. (b) 24 groups. (c) 10 pens and 7 notebooks per group.

runtime_row.answer: Compute cumulative frequencies, locate median class (N/2), then use median formula: L + [(N/2 − cf)/f]×h.
runtime_row.explanation: Standard median-of-grouped-data procedure.
solutionSteps: First, create a cumulative frequency (cf) column: Classes: 0-10 (f=5, cf=5), 10-20 (f=7, cf=12), 20-30 (f=12, cf=24), 30-40 (f=9, cf=33), 40-50 (f=7, cf=40).; Calculate N (total frequency) = 5+7+12+9+7 = 40. Then, N/2 = 40/2 = 20. [1]

Identify the median class: The class whose cumulative frequency is just greater than or equal to N/2 (20). This is the 20-30 class (cf=24).; From the median class (20-30): Lower limit (L) = 20, Frequency (f) = 12, Class size (h) = 10. Cumulative frequency of the preceding class (cf) = 12. [1]
runtime_row.finalAnswer: Compute cumulative frequencies, locate median class (N/2), then use median formula: L + [(N/2 − cf)/f]×h.

runtime_row.questionText: A teacher computed the mean height of 40 students using grouped data method. If Σfi = 40 and Σ(fi × xi) = 1680, but later found an error where one frequency was recorded as 8 instead of 5, find the correct mean.
solutionSteps: Given: Mean = Σ(fi × xi) / Σfi = 1680 / 40 = 42
Error: frequency recorded as 8 instead of 5
Difference in frequency = 5 - 8 = -3
Assume class midpoint of error class = x
Correct Σ(fi × xi) = 1680 - 8x + 5x = 1680 - 3x
Need additional info about class or use:
Impact on sum = -3x, if midpoint = 40: Σ = 1680 - 120 = 1560
Correct mean = 1560 / 40 = 39 (example with x=40)

runtime_row.subject: Maths
runtime_row.questionText: Design a grouped frequency distribution over four equal classes of width 10 (starting at 0) such that the mode is exactly 25. Specify the frequencies and verify using the mode formula.
solutionSteps: Choose modal class 20-30 (so l = 20, h = 10) and target mode = 25.
Mode = l + ((f₁ − f₀)/(2f₁ − f₀ − f₂)) × h = 20 + ((f₁ − f₀)/(2f₁ − f₀ − f₂)) × 10 = 25.
So (f₁ − f₀)/(2f₁ − f₀ − f₂) = 1/2 ⇒ 2(f₁ − f₀) = 2f₁ − f₀ − f₂ ⇒ −2f₀ = −f₀ − f₂ ⇒ f₂ = f₀.
Pick f₀ = 5, f₂ = 5, f₁ = 12 (must be max). And another class 30-40 with f₃ = 4 (less than f₂ so modal class is unique). Final: 0-10 → 5, 10-20 → 5, 20-30 → 12, 30-40 → 4.

Check: max freq 12 in 20-30 ⇒ modal class confirmed. Mode = 20 + ((12 − 5)/(24 − 5 − 4)) × 10 = 20 + (7/15) × 10 ≈ 24.67 — close to 25 but not exact. To get exactly 25, set f₂ = f₀ as derived above and try f₀ = 5, f₂ = 5, f₁ = 11: 2f₁ − f₀ − f₂ = 22 − 10 = 12; (f₁ − f₀) = 6; ratio 6/12 = 1/2 ⇒ Mode = 20 + 5 = 25. ✓ Final distribution: 0-10 → 0, 10-20 → 5, 20-30 → 11, 30-40 → 5.
runtime_row.finalAnswer: Frequencies 0, 5, 11, 5 over classes 0-10, 10-20, 20-30, 30-40 give Mode = 25 exactly.
runtime_row.strategyHint: Symmetric flanking frequencies (f₀ = f₂) place the mode at l + h/2.

solutionSteps: Assertion (A) is true: by definition, the modal class of grouped data is the class interval with the highest frequency. [½]
Reason (R) is true: Mode = L + [(f₁−f₀)/(2f₁−f₀−f₂)]·h is the NCERT formula for the mode of grouped data, where L is the lower limit of the modal class. [½]

R presupposes the modal class (it needs L and f₁ from it); it does not explain why the modal class is chosen as the class of highest frequency. Hence both are true but R is not the correct explanation of A. [1]
runtime_row.finalAnswer: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

runtime_row.questionText: Two rectangular sheets of dimensions 45 cm × 155 cm are folded to make hollow right circular cylindrical pipes with exactly 1 cm overlap when sticking the ends. Sheet 1 is folded along its length, Sheet 2 along its width. Both pipes are closed on both ends. (i) Find the difference in curved surface areas of the two cylinders. (ii) Find the ratio of the volumes of the two cylinders formed. (Use π = 22/7.) OR (i) How many cylindrical cans (with the geometry shown) can be packed in a cubical container with no more cans fitting? (ii) If one can capacity = 539 ml, find the internal volume of the cubical container.
runtime_row.answer: (i) 110 cm^2 difference. (ii) Ratio V1:V2 from MS. [OR] (i) 32 cans. (ii) 21952 cm^3.
solutionSteps: [1 mark] Variant 1 (i): Sheet 1 makes a pipe of height 155 cm; the 1 cm overlap wastes 155 × 1 = 155 cm². Sheet 2 makes a pipe of height 45 cm; overlap wastes 45 × 1 = 45 cm².
[1 mark] Difference in curved surface area = 155 − 45 = 110 cm².
[1 mark] (ii) Sheet 1 circumference = 45 − 1 = 44 cm ⟹ r₁ = 7 cm; Sheet 2 circumference = 155 − 1 = 154 cm ⟹ r₂ = 49/2 cm.
[1 mark] (ii) Ratio of volumes V₁ : V₂ = (r₁²·h₁)/(r₂²·h₂) = (7²·155)/((49/2)²·45) = 124 : 441.
[1 mark] OR variant: container side = 2p with 4 cans per direction ⟹ 4 × 4 × 2 = 32 cans; with can capacity 539 ml, p = 14 cm, cube side = 28 cm, internal volume = 28³ = 21952 cm³.
runtime_row.finalAnswer: (i) Δ CSA = 110 cm^2; ratio from formula. [OR] 32 cans; 21952 cm^3.

runtime_row.questionText: A vessel is in the form of an inverted cone. Its height is 8 cm and the radius of its top, which is open, is 5 cm. It is filled with water up to the brim. When lead shots, each of which is a sphere of radius 0·5 cm, are dropped into the vessel, onefourth of the water flows out. Find the number of lead shots dropped in the vessel. 3 4 3 4=12
runtime_row.answer: Volume of water in the cone = (1/3)π × 5² × 8 = 200π/3 cm³; water that flows out = (1/4) × 200π/3 = 50π/3 cm³; volume of one lead shot = (4/3)π(1/2)³ = π/6 cm³; number of lead shots = (50π/3) ÷ (π/6) = 100
solutionSteps: [1 mark] Radius of cone r = 5 cm, height h = 8 cm. Volume of water filling the cone = (1/3)πr²h = (1/3) × π × 5² × 8 = 200π/3 cm³.
[1 mark] Volume of water that flows out = (1/4) × (200π/3) = 50π/3 cm³.
[1 mark] Radius of each lead shot = 0.5 cm = 1/2 cm. Volume of one lead shot = (4/3)π(1/2)³ = π/6 cm³.
[1 mark] Number of lead shots = (volume of water displaced)/(volume of one lead shot) = (50π/3) ÷ (π/6) = (50π/3) × (6/π).
[1 mark] = 100. Hence 100 lead shots were dropped into the vessel.

runtime_row.questionText: From a solid cylinder whose height is 2.8 cm and radius 2.1 cm, a conical cavity of the same height and same radius is hollowed out. Find the volume and the total surface area of the remaining solid.

[1 mark] Total surface area of remaining solid = CSA of cylinder + CSA of cone + area of top circular base = 2πrh + πrl + πr² = 2 × (22/7) × 2.1 × 2.8 + (22/7) × 2.1 × 3.5 + (22/7) × 2.1 × 2.1.

runtime_row.questionText: A vessel is in the form of an inverted cone of height 8 cm and top radius 5 cm, open at the top and filled with water to the brim. Lead shots — each a sphere of radius 0.5 cm — are dropped in, and one-fourth of the water flows out. Find the number of lead shots dropped into the vessel. (Take π = 22/7.)
solutionSteps: Volume of the cone (water initially) = (1/3)πR²H = (1/3)π(5)²(8) cm³ = 200π/3 cm³.
Water displaced = (1/4) × cone volume = (1/4)(200π/3) = 50π/3 cm³.
Volume of one lead shot = (4/3)π(0.5)³ = (4/3)π(0.125) = π/6 cm³.
runtime_row.strategyHint: Displaced water = (1/4) of cone volume = N × (volume of one sphere); solve for N.

runtime_row.subject: Maths
runtime_row.questionText: In the figure, ΔABC is a right-angled triangle, such that: AC = 25 cm, PT ∥ AB and SR ∥ BC. Find the area of ΔPQR.
solutionSteps: [1 mark] From the figure: RC = 50/5 = 10 cm and PC = 50/3 cm, so PR = PC − RC = 50/3 − 10 = 20/3 cm.
[1 mark] Since QR ∥ BC (as SR ∥ BC), ΔPQR ~ ΔPTC by the Basic Proportionality Theorem, giving PR/CR = PQ/QT.
[1 mark] In right ΔPQR, by Pythagoras QR² = PR² − PQ² = (20/3)² − (16/3)² = (400 − 256)/9 = 144/9 ⟹ QR = 4 cm.
[1 mark] Area of ΔPQR = ½ × QR × PQ = ½ × 4 × 16/3 = 32/3 cm².
runtime_row.strategyHint: REQUIRES-FIGURE: right triangle ABC with internal lines PT and SR.

runtime_row.questionText: If ∠ACB = ∠CDA in a figure with C on segment BD (or with the standard NCERT/Exemplar configuration), AC = 8 cm and AD = 3 cm, find BD.

Correspondence: A↔A, C↔D, B↔C ⇒ AC/AD = AB/AC.
AC² = AD · AB ⇒ 64 = 3 · AB ⇒ AB = 64/3 cm.
